It is not a Jury's job to determine whether someone is "innocent". Their purpose is to decide whether they think an accused is guilty or not-guilty. Guilty means "Hey government, please remove this person from society." Not-guilty means "Whatever the law, whatever anyone said about him, whatever he may have done or not done, I can't say he should be removed from society."

It takes unanimous consent from TWELVE random people to find someone guilty for the State to remove the accused from society. It only takes ONE of those twelve to think that the person shouldn't be removed from society to stop the State from doing so. If just one of the twelve insists he is guilty, or just one insists he is not-guilty, the trial is over. If it is a mistrial the government can try their case with a different jury or eventually just give up trying to prosecute the accused. But to ever actually put the guy away for good, a full group of twelve must agree that he is guilty.

The US jury system is actually pretty unique in history. It is based on ancient British customs where local communities determined whether or not someone should be punished. This system was suspended when William the Conqueror and the Normans (vikings who had conquered part of France and partially assimilated into their culture) took over Britain and replaced the ancient custom with punishments dictated by the new line of royalty. Centuries later as people rebelled against the King's powers, the Jury system was eventually reinstituted in the USA as a guard against tyrannical abuse by a central government detached from local communities.

But most Americans have no fucking idea what is going on when they sit on a jury. Most seriously believe their job is simply to determine whether the accused broke the law. That isn't the point at all - career investigators and prosecutors and judges and the various experts employed in the justice system don't need 12 random idiots to help them decide whether someone broke the law or not; the only thing a jury would be good for if that were the case would be helping prevent an evil government from persecuting people for political or economic purposes. But the point of the jury is much deeper than that.

A jury doesn't just rule on whether someone broke the law, they also rule on whether the law itself is just, and whether the prosecution of the law was just. No matter what the State says, it is ultimately up to those twelve random people to decide whether the accused should be removed from society. If a juror doesn't think a law is just, they can rule not-guilty. If a juror thinks a prosecutor or cop was unjust in an investigation or in bringing charges, they can rule not-guilty.

Even if a juror thinks that the law and prosecution was just, thinks the accused committed the crime, yet thinks the accused nevertheless should still be allowed to stay in society, that juror can rule not-guilty. The juror doesn't have to give his reasons for thinking this to anyone. He can just sit there and say "Not-guilty", cross his arms, and not say another word to anyone else.

If you sit on a jury and rule "Guilty" for ANY reason, you are making the ultimate determination that the accused should be removed from your society. Most people don't understand the awesome responsibility and power that rests with them when they sit on a jury; they like to shirk that responsibility by thinking that they are just helping the government make a fair call, thinking the government is really responsible for making that decision. That's not the case. It is entirely the judgment of the jury, by ruling guilty that gives the government permission to remove the accused from society.
